transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2028-11-08 14:00 UTC
- Duration: ~46 minutes
- Attendees: Alyssa (AE), Diego (SE), Priya (CSM) — Firestone: Maya, Ravi, Jonas, Lena

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect):
Redwood and Firestone walk through the latest bench runs; incumbent shows slightly lower 99th p90 in steady-state but Redwood has better tail behavior under burst when KV cache is primed. Discussion centers on quantise/quantization choices, continuous batching, and fallback routing to an incumbent-compatible variant. Security asks for SOC two docs and KMS details. Next steps decided: run a 1-hour dedicated slot with priming script, share cost ladder and schedule follow-up.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alyssa (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we, uh, wanted to kick off with the week-overweek bench summary. Diego will run through the numbers and then we'll talk routing and next steps.
[00:18] Diego (SE): Cool, so quick preface — these were three runs: steady QPS 200, burst to 1k for ten minutes, and a mixed diurnal trace. Baseline is IncumbentAI as you know. For steady 200 qps our p50 is comparable, p90/in tail we saw 12% better on Redwood when KV cache hits were above 90%. But when the cache warmed down, there were spikes.
[00:40] Maya (Firestone): Sorry can you repeat the cache bit — you mean K-V cache? We saw in our lab that after cold start there's like a 400 ms penalty sometimes.
[00:51] Diego (SE): Yeah, K-V cache, sometimes the transcription shows K-V cash, hah. But yes, if the KV cache isn't primed we see tokenization and I/O causing a latency cliff. The fix we tested is priming and a small initial-batch warmup to reduce misses.
[01:12] Jonas (Infra): On our side we saw NVMe I/O saturation during the burst run, that correlated with the spike windows. Is that something you observed in Redwood infra logs?
[01:25] Diego (SE): We did see elevated I/O waits in that run — looks like the model shard swap activity increased under unprimed loads. We're tuning kernel and also testing a quantize variant that reduces model size for faster swappage.
[01:40] Ravi (CTO): How's the quantize option affect quality? Our main success criteria is parity with current vendor on top-1 accuracy for clinical entity extraction.
[01:51] Diego (SE): Good question. The quantized variant we trialed (8-bit dynamic) had micro-drops on few-shot entity recall — maybe 1.5% absolute on our eval set. We can run the customer prompt set to validate. Prioritizing batching and caching keeps quality unchanged but improves cost/latency.
[02:12] Alyssa (AE): Just to ground, the customer's SLAs are p95 < 220 ms for inference under normal load and p99 < 450 ms under burst, right? Is that still the stated goal?
[02:27] Maya (Firestone): Correct, p95 220ms target is the one we care about. p99 under burst ideally under 500ms.
[02:36] Priya (CSM): Noted. Our lab vs production differences — remember your traffic has a high variance with short-lived spikes from batch jobs, that pattern exacerbates cold cache.
[02:48] Alyssa (AE): On the cost side, we prepared a 'cost ladder' showing token-unit economics across three routing policies: 1) always-hosted, 2) prioritized-dedicated-with-burst-fallback, 3) incumbent-fallback-heavy. Diego will walk through estimated per-1M-token costs.
[03:05] Diego (SE): Right — raw numbers: hosted steady ~ $1.10/1M tokens (est), dedicated reserved drops to ~$0.70/1M tokens at commit, but remember dedicated has slot contention and the small priming overhead. Incumbent currently billing you at $0.95/1M tokens on their peak plan. So the cost delta depends a lot on how often you hit cold-cache spikes.
[03:28] Lena (Security): Quick pause — we'll need SOC2, encryption at rest with customer-managed KMS, and SSO/SAML for the admin console. Also audit logs with 90-day retention at minimum.
[03:44] Alyssa (AE): Understood — we'll attach our SOC2 and the KMS integration guide. We support AWS KMS, GCP CMEK, and there's a HSM path for private deployments.
[03:56] Lena (Security): For on-prem or VPC we need names of the KMS vendors and whether keys are rotated automatically, that's important for our audit.
[04:07] Diego (SE): I'll pull the KMS config page and add notes on rotation. Also, on the networking question — for Private we can run in a customer VPC with private endpoints.
[04:15] Jonas (Infra): Back to the benchmark: can Redwood simulate our mixed diurnal pattern with the same QPS bursts? We want a head-to-head with the incumbent under the exact traffic trace.
[04:27] Diego (SE): Yes we can. In fact we recommended a 1-hour dedicated-slot run with your exact trace plus our KV-priming script to show the best-case tail numbers. That's what we'd like to schedule next.
[04:39] Maya (Firestone): Great — how long is the priming window? We worry about priming cost overhead.
[04:45] Diego (SE): Priming is typically the first 2-5 minutes of sustained requests to reach a 90%+ hit rate for the KV cache depending on prompt variety. We'll include a priming-only phase in the dedicated slot so you can quantify overhead.
[04:58] Ravi (CTO): If priming is needed, does Redwood support rehydration or persistent cache across warm restarts? We don't want priming every deploy.
[05:09] Diego (SE): We have persistent KV cache for dedicated/private options; hosted ephemeral nodes can't guarantee persisted cache across cold restarts, but we do have region-level warm pools and sticky routing to reduce churn.
[05:22] Alyssa (AE): For decisioning we propose two experiments: 1) dedicated-slot run with priming and full trace; 2) hosted run without priming to show production-like behavior. Compare p50/p90/p99 and unit cost.
[05:36] Maya (Firestone): That sounds fair. Also we need the quality-eval using our prompts. We can run it client-side but would prefer you test end-to-end.
[05:46] Diego (SE): We'll run the eval against the same checkpoints and include token-level logs. Be aware the transcription of our logs sometimes scrubs model names, the export might show RedwoodModel-v1 as RMv1 or R-M one — small thing but it happens in reports.
[06:03] Jonas (Infra): Regarding the NVMe I/O spike earlier, any quick tunables we can try? On our infra side we can increase IOPS, but curious if you have batching/window tweaks?
[06:14] Diego (SE): Two immediate levers: lower max-batch-size so peak memory swap is less aggressive, and increase prefix caching TTL to reduce shard reloads. Both reduce I/O at the cost of slight latency change in some tails.
[06:28] Maya (Firestone): Can you quantify "slight"? Our SLO is tight.
[06:33] Diego (SE): From our experiments, lowering max-batch from 64 to 32 reduced I/O spikes and improved p99 under burst by ~120ms, p95 was largely unchanged, throughput dropped about 6% in steady-state. We can provide exact numbers after the dedicated run.
[06:53] Ravi (CTO): Incumbent claim they have a better p95 under burst due to their custom caching layer. Any plan to do a side-by-side with the exact same cache behavior?
[07:03] Diego (SE): We can attempt to emulate their caching policy but there are infra-level differences. Our approach is to show realistic workload with priming vs non-priming and then present routing playbooks: prefer Redwood during steady and failover to incumbent for extreme unprimed spikes — that gives you cost savings while preserving SLA.
[07:22] Priya (CSM): Just to add — routing policies can be automated: e.g., if observed tail latency > threshold, switch to incumbent for next N minutes. We'll help codify those thresholds.
[07:33] Maya (Firestone): That automation is appealing but operationally we want visibility. Dashboards? Traces?
[07:38] Alyssa (AE): Redwood Console exports dashboards per route/model and we can give you a shared view. We'll set up a read-only dashboard and tracer links for incidents.
[07:50] Lena (Security): For the audit trail we need immutable request logs for 90 days — are those available?
[07:57] Diego (SE): Yes, request-level audit logs are available for dedicated/private; hosted can ship logs to your SIEM (via forwarder) with retention as configured. We'll include the log retention SLA in the doc.
[08:09] Jonas (Infra): Ok, let's lock timing. We can give you a 1-hour dedicated slot next Wednesday 2028-11-09 between 02:00-06:00 UTC. Which one works for Redwood?
[08:20] Alyssa (AE): Diego, you ok to run that window?
[08:22] Diego (SE): Yep, I can run the dedicated slot at 03:00 UTC on 2028-11-09. I'll include the priming script and the specific ping endpoints for log collection.
[08:31] Maya (Firestone): Perfect. A couple of other minor things — can you send the SOC two and KMS integration link to my security alias?
[08:39] Alyssa (AE): Yes, we'll email SOC2, KMS guide, and the cost-ladder spreadsheet after the call.
[08:45] Priya (CSM): Also, timeline check — do we have a decision gate after the dedicated-slot result? What is your procurement window?
[08:54] Ravi (CTO): We're targeting a vendor decision by end of November. If the dedicated-slot shows parity and cost savings, we'll move to contracting and private deployment evaluation.
[09:06] Diego (SE): One more note on quantize: if quality doesn't meet your bar, we keep full precision but tune batching and routing. Quantize is an optional lever for additional unit-cost wins.
[09:18] Maya (Firestone): Understood.
[09:22] Alyssa (AE): Alright, let's recap next steps...
[09:25] Alyssa (AE): Action items — Diego runs the dedicated slot at 03:00 UTC Nov 9, Diego to share logs. Maya provides traffic trace. Alyssa to send cost ladder and SOC2 + KMS guide. Priya to set follow-up meeting after the run.
[09:44] Maya (Firestone): Thanks everyone, that wraps it up.

Notes: occasional transcription artifacts (e.g., S-L-O's for SLOs, K-V cash for KV cache). Some speaker tags may be assigned generically by the recorder.
